items.q: A launch involves four teams with conflicting priorities and no shared deadline. Your first move as TPM is…
choices: Build a shared milestone plan with named owners and a decision log
Collect each team's dates and average them
items.explain: Alignment starts with a shared plan and explicit ownership. Meetings and escalation without a plan just add noise.

items.q: A dependency team says their API will slip two weeks. The best response is…
choices: Quietly absorb the slip and hope
Re-plan the critical path, surface options and tradeoffs to stakeholders, and negotiate scope or dates
Name them in the status report
items.explain: Slips are managed, not hidden: re-plan, present options with tradeoffs, and renegotiate explicitly.

items.q: A status report is most useful when it…
choices: Leads with decisions needed and risks, not activity logs
items.explain: Decision-makers need decisions-needed and risks up front. Activity logs bury the signal.

items.q: ‘Influence without authority’ most reliably comes from…
choices: Being the loudest voice in the room
Owning the plan, the data, and the follow-through so teams trust your coordination
items.explain: Influence is earned through reliable coordination: clear plans, honest data, and relentless follow-through.

items.q: In a technical design review, the TPM's highest-value contribution is…
choices: Asking how the design affects milestones, dependencies, and rollout risk — and ensuring the answers get recorded
Staying silent; it is engineering's call
items.explain: The TPM translates technical choices into program consequences: schedule, dependencies, and launch risk.

items.q: A program is red on two milestones. You…
choices: Diagnose root causes, re-forecast honestly, and bring a recovery plan with options
Wait for it to resolve itself
Reassign blame in the next review
items.explain: Honest reds with a recovery plan build trust; hidden reds become missed launches.

items.q: A strong engineer is missing deadlines and seems disengaged. Your first step is…
choices: Start a performance improvement plan immediately
Have a candid 1:1 to understand what changed before diagnosing
Ignore it and hope it passes
items.explain: Diagnose before prescribing. A candid 1:1 surfaces whether it is workload, motivation, or something personal — each needs a different response.

items.q: Your team consistently over-commits and misses. You…
choices: Push harder on the same plan
Introduce capacity-based planning with historical velocity and protected slack
items.explain: Over-commitment is a planning-system failure. Capacity planning grounded in real velocity fixes the system instead of blaming the team.

items.q: In hiring, the highest-signal practice is…
choices: A structured loop with a defined bar, calibrated interviewers, and written feedback
items.explain: Structure beats instinct: defined bars, calibrated interviewers, and written feedback before discussion reduce bias and raise the bar.

items.q: Tech debt is visibly slowing the team. You…
choices: Quantify the drag, prioritize debt against features with product, and fund it as strategy
Ignore it until it becomes an incident
items.explain: Debt is a business tradeoff. Quantify the cost, put it on the roadmap next to features, and fund it deliberately.

items.q: During a production incident, the EM's job is…
choices: To coordinate: clear roles, communication, and customer updates while engineers debug
To wait quietly for the postmortem
items.explain: The EM runs the incident: roles, comms, and customer updates. Engineers debug better when someone else coordinates.

items.q: A promotion case for your report needs…
choices: Your gut feeling that they are ready
Documented impact against the level's expectations, peer evidence, and calibration
items.explain: Promotions are argued with evidence: impact mapped to level expectations, peer signal, and calibration — not tenure or vibes.

items.q: ‘Design an app for booking dog walkers.’ The best opening is…
choices: Clarify the user, the problem, and what success looks like before solutions
items.explain: Structure starts with user, problem, and success criteria. Solutions before framing is the classic failure mode.

items.q: Two features, one sprint of capacity. You…
choices: Compare expected impact versus effort with stated assumptions, and pick the higher-leverage bet
items.explain: Prioritization is impact over effort with explicit assumptions — so the decision can be revisited when assumptions change.

items.q: Activation dropped 15% after a redesign. Your first move is…
choices: Segment the data — which users, which step, when — before concluding
items.explain: Debug before reacting: segment by cohort, step, and time to find whether it is the redesign, a segment, or noise.

items.q: A good success metric is…
choices: Tied to user value and movable by the team, with a clear time window
items.explain: Metrics must track real user value, be influenceable by the team, and be bounded in time — vanity totals fail all three.

items.q: An A/B test shows +2% conversion at p=0.4. You…
choices: Treat it as inconclusive: not statistically significant
Keep peeking until it turns significant
items.explain: p=0.4 means the result is indistinguishable from noise. Shipping noise as signal is how teams fool themselves.

items.q: ‘Tell me about a conflict with engineering.’ The strongest structure is…
choices: STAR — situation, task, action, result — with your role and what you would do differently
Say you have never had a conflict
items.explain: STAR with your actual role and honest learning shows self-awareness; blame or denial shows neither.

items.q: A stakeholder demands a feature that data says users do not want. You…
choices: Build it to keep the peace
Share the evidence, probe the underlying need, and align on an experiment
items.explain: Influence through evidence: surface the data, find the real need behind the request, and propose a test.

items.q: An engineer says ‘we need to add a cache.’ As a technical PM you first ask…
choices: What read pattern and latency requirement motivates it, and what staleness is acceptable
items.explain: Caching is a tradeoff: hit patterns, latency goals, and staleness tolerance determine whether it helps or adds a new failure mode.

items.q: Designing a public API, the most important early decision is…
choices: The resource model and versioning strategy, because they lock in compatibility promises
items.explain: Resource model and versioning are nearly irreversible; they define the contract every integrator builds against.

items.q: To size ‘how many users hit this endpoint daily,’ you would…
choices: Query the event data or ask for the analytics table
Use marketing site traffic as a proxy
items.explain: Technical PMs answer sizing questions with data: the event stream or analytics table, not proxies.

items.q: Build versus buy for an internal tool: the decisive factors are…
choices: Which is more fun to build
Total cost, differentiation, maintenance burden, and strategic control
items.explain: Build-versus-buy is total cost plus strategy: maintenance burden and control matter as much as the sticker price.

items.q: A partner integration keeps breaking. Your move is…
choices: Define the contract — SLAs, error codes, webhooks versus polling — instrument failures, and align on a fix with the partner
Rebuild it yourself over the weekend
items.explain: Flaky integrations are contract problems: define expectations, instrument the failures, then fix jointly.

items.q: In a system design discussion, the PM's distinctive contribution is…
choices: Connecting architecture choices to user outcomes, cost, and iteration speed — and recording the tradeoffs
items.explain: The PM translates architecture into consequences: what users feel, what it costs, how fast the team can change it.

items.q: A user asks your LLM feature a question it cannot answer. The best UX is…
choices: Communicate uncertainty, show sources, and offer a path forward
Reply ‘I don't know’ with no further help
items.explain: Uncertainty is a design input: show what the system knows, cite sources, and give the user a next step.

items.q: Before launching an AI summary feature, the highest-value evaluation is…
choices: A golden dataset of representative inputs with human-judged quality criteria, run on every model or prompt change
items.explain: Golden datasets with judged criteria turn quality from vibes into a regression-testable property.

items.q: RAG is the right pattern when…
choices: You want the model to answer from your private, changing documents with citations
You have no data at all
items.explain: RAG grounds answers in retrieved documents — ideal for private, changing corpora where citations matter.

items.q: Your AI feature's cost per user is 10x the subscription price. You…
choices: Ship anyway and hope for scale
Redesign — smaller model, caching, shorter contexts, or a different price tier — before scaling
Hide the cost in another budget line
items.explain: Unit economics are a product constraint: fix the cost structure (model size, caching, context) before scaling losses.

items.q: A red-team test shows the model can be prompted to reveal internal instructions. You…
choices: Ignore it; users will not find it
Treat it as a launch blocker: harden inputs, add output filters and least-privilege tool access, then retest
items.explain: Prompt-injection exposure is a launch blocker: mitigate with input handling, output controls, and tool least-privilege, then re-verify.

items.q: ‘Hallucination’ in product terms means…
choices: The model generates plausible-sounding but false content, so outputs need grounding or verification where accuracy matters
items.explain: Hallucination is confident falsehood: design grounding, citations, or human verification wherever accuracy matters.

items.q: When choosing between building on an API versus fine-tuning, the PM should weigh…
choices: Data needs, cost, latency, control, and how fast base models are improving — API first unless there is a durable reason
Always fine-tune; it is more impressive
items.explain: Default to the API: fine-tuning earns its place only with durable data advantages, latency needs, or cost math that survives the next base-model release.
